note_on_method: Only the two filters that actually qualify in Seattle are written. /indoor/ has no entry because Seattle has zero indoor courts; /free/ and /public/ have none because fee_type and access_type are unstated on every venue. Writing intros for pages that cannot exist would be writing for a URL nobody can reach.

slots.why_this_filter: In Seattle this list is the entire directory. All twenty-four venues in the city are outdoor, every one of the ninety-two courts is open to the sky, and not a single one is covered or climate controlled. In the records that could be confirmed, Seattle has no indoor pickleball at all. Indoor courts do exist inside community centres and private clubs, but none has been checked against a named source, so none is listed anywhere on this site. Pickleball in Seattle is a weather-dependent activity, and this page says so rather than implying otherwise.
slots.what_qualifies:
A venue appears here when Seattle Parks records at least one outdoor court at it. That is the whole test. Venues whose outdoor court count is not stated do not appear. Since every Seattle venue qualifies, this list and the city page currently hold the same twenty-four venues.

Outdoor does not tell you much on its own. Eighteen of the twenty-five locations Seattle Parks records are striped for tennis and pickleball on the same surface, three share with basketball or badminton, and only four are dedicated pickleball. So an outdoor court in Seattle is usually a tennis court with extra lines on it, shared with whoever booked it. The city publishes no surface type and no condition assessment for any of them, so whether the asphalt is fresh or cracked is not known for any location on this list.

faqs.q: Is there anywhere indoors to play in Seattle?
faqs.a: Not stated. Several community centres and private clubs in Seattle have indoor courts and they are very probably real, but none has been checked against a named source, so none appears on this site. If you know of one and can point at a source, the correction link on any page reaches a real queue.

You do not play, at any of these twenty-four venues. None is covered and none is climate controlled. That is the single biggest gap in Seattle pickleball as this directory currently records it, and no amount of filtering fixes it.

faqs.q: Do I need to book an outdoor court?
faqs.a: Seattle Parks publishes no reservation information in the pickleball dataset, so the answer is not known. Eighteen of these sites share their surface with tennis, and tennis courts in the city are bookable, so arriving to find a booked court is a real possibility.

slots.why_this_filter:
Seattle loses the light early. In late December sunset is before half past four, so for a large part of the year an unlit court is a court you can use at lunchtime and not after work. Five of the twenty-four venues have lighting recorded by the city: Bitter Lake Playfield and Rainier Beach Playfield with eight courts each, Miller Playfield with five, and Alki Playground and Mt. Baker Park with four each. That is the entire evening capacity of pickleball in Seattle, and between them they hold twenty-nine of the city's ninety-two courts.

One caveat. Mt. Baker Park is lit but also carries a city-imposed 10 p.m. curfew after noise studies found play exceeding Seattle Municipal Code chapter 25.08, so its lights are less useful late than the raw fact suggests. Bitter Lake and Rainier Beach carry no such order in the records checked.
slots.what_qualifies:
A venue appears here only where Seattle Parks has positively recorded lighting as present. Where the city says nothing about lighting, the venue is absent from this list and shows lights as not stated on its own page, because an unchecked court and a dark court are different things. Nineteen of the twenty-four Seattle venues are recorded as having no lights.

Seattle Parks records that lighting exists; it does not record what hours the lights run, whether they are on a timer, or whether they are switched on at all outside the tennis season. No source has been found that states any of that for any of the five venues. These are the five places where evening play is possible in principle, not five places where the lights are guaranteed to be on when you arrive in February. Three of the five (Bitter Lake, Rainier Beach and Miller Playfield) also carry dedicated parking and all-year restrooms, which makes them the more practical winter options of the group.

faqs.q: Which of the five is best for a winter evening?
faqs.a: On the recorded facts, Bitter Lake Playfield or Rainier Beach Playfield: eight courts each, lights, nets, dedicated parking and an all-year restroom, and neither carries the 10 p.m. curfew that applies at Mt. Baker Park. This is a reading of the city's data, not a recommendation from experience.

faqs.q: Do the lights stay on until the park closes?
faqs.a: Unknown. Seattle Parks records that lighting exists but publishes nothing about operating hours, timers or seasonal switching. Treat these as places where evening play is possible rather than guaranteed.

faqs.q: Why are only five venues listed when nineteen others exist?
faqs.a: Because the city records no lighting at those nineteen. Most of them are genuinely unlit rather than unchecked, but we keep the two ideas separate everywhere on this site: a venue only reaches this list when lighting is positively recorded, never when it is merely not ruled out.

sources.evidence: LIGHTED = Yes at Bitter Lake Playfield (8), Rainier Beach Playfield (8), Miller Playfield (5), Alki Playground (4) and Mt. Baker Park (4). INDOOROUTDOOR = Outdoor at all 25 recorded locations; no covered or climate-control field exists in the layer.

Mt. Baker Park is one of three sites limited to 7 a.m.-10 p.m. weekdays and 9 a.m.-10 p.m. weekends from 15 September 2025, after noise studies with SDCI found levels exceeding Seattle Municipal Code Chapter 25.08.
